entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Albrecht Dürer the Elder (1427–1502) was a master goldsmith and entrepreneur whose esteemed workshop in Nuremberg, a vibrant center of late medieval European trade and craftsmanship, laid the foundational artistic and economic environment for his son, the renowned artist Albrecht Dürer the Younger. Born in Ajtós, Hungary, Dürer the Elder migrated to Nuremberg in 1455, establishing a highly successful goldsmith business that catered to the city's affluent merchant class and aristocracy. His life spanned a pivotal era marked by the decline of feudalism, the rise of powerful urban centers, and the burgeoning influence of the Renaissance in Northern Europe, positioning him as a representative figure of the era's skilled artisan-entrepreneur.

His journey from Hungary to Nuremberg, following an apprenticeship in goldsmithing, marked a significant professional and personal transformation. By 1467, he had established his own workshop and married Barbara Holper, with whom he had eighteen children, including Albrecht Dürer the Younger, born in 1471. Dürer the Elder's workshop specialized in intricate gold and silver pieces, often incorporating religious motifs and heraldic designs, reflecting both the spiritual devotion and social aspirations of his clientele. His meticulous craftsmanship and entrepreneurial acumen allowed him to prosper, providing his large family with a secure livelihood and his children with opportunities for education and apprenticeships, crucial for the development of his famous son.

entities.summary:
Albrecht Dürer the Elder (born 1427 in Ajtós, Kingdom of Hungary; died 1502 in Nuremberg, Holy Roman Empire) was a master goldsmith and entrepreneur whose establishment of a prominent workshop in Nuremberg laid the economic and artisanal foundation for one of the most celebrated artistic dynasties of the Northern Renaissance. Operating within the vibrant mercantile environment of a Free Imperial City, Dürer the Elder navigated the complexities of late Medieval craft guilds and burgeoning capitalist practices, becoming a respected figure in the city's robust economy. His career spanned a period marked by significant cultural exchange between Central Europe and Italy, though his primary influence was rooted in the German goldsmithing tradition.

His primary achievement was the establishment and successful operation of a sophisticated goldsmith workshop in Nuremberg, producing intricate devotional objects, jewelry, and other luxury items for a discerning clientele. This enterprise thrived, enabling him to acquire significant property and establish a stable household. Crucially, he recognized and nurtured the prodigious artistic talent of his son, Albrecht Dürer the Younger, providing him with initial training in goldsmithing before apprenticing him to the painter Michael Wolgemut in 1486. This pivotal decision, made by a craftsman who himself possessed considerable artistic skill, redirected his son towards painting and printmaking, ultimately shaping the course of European art.
